c.tagline: Belle-epoque bay city — golden Sardinero sand and Renzo Piano's Centro Botin.

taxi.fareNote: Taxis are white with a diagonal blue stripe and metered. Uber has only a limited presence in the city; Cabify and Free Now are the usual ride-hailing apps, and street hails or taxi ranks work well.

emergency.note: 112 is the single EU-wide emergency number connecting to police, fire and ambulance across Spain.

avoid.reason: Occasional petty theft around the train/bus stations and in summer crowds at El Sardinero beach.

hood_desc: The commercial and civic heart around the cathedral, the Jardines de Pereda and Renzo Piano's waterfront Centro Botin arts centre; the best walkable base, with shops, the ferry terminal and stations close by.
A former fishing harbour turned pretty leisure marina lined with seafood terraces and moored boats; relaxed, central and within easy reach of everything.
An elegant belle-epoque beach resort with two long golden strands, the Gran Casino and grand seaside villas and cafes; airy and upscale.

water.note: Tap water is safe and of good quality.

transit.hours: City buses run roughly 6:30am-11pm, with a reduced night-bus (buho) network at weekends; taxis cover the small hours.
transit.note: Compact and walkable along the bay, Santander is easily covered on foot; buses are mainly useful for reaching El Sardinero, La Magdalena and the outer neighbourhoods.
transit.pay: A single TUS bus ride is about EUR 1.30 in cash on board; a rechargeable TUS card lowers the fare and lets you transfer, and contactless bank cards work on newer buses. The little Los Reginas launches across the bay to Somo and Pedreña are paid at the quay.

bus: Estacion de Autobuses de Santander (ALSA/FlixBus intercity coaches)
ferry: Los Reginas bay launches to Somo & Pedreña

transit.m: ALSA airport bus to the city bus station (~15 min, every 30 min)

tip.r: Service is included; rounding up or leaving 5-10% for good restaurant service is appreciated but never expected.

food.name: Rabas
food.desc: Strips of squid in a light batter, fried fast and eaten with lemon and a beer. Cantabria's ritual pre-lunch snack, ordered by the racion.

places.name: Marucho
places.note: Small tiled bar with a long reputation for squid and market seafood.

places.name: Bodega La Conveniente
places.note: Cavernous old bodega near Canadio; barrels, piano and generous raciones.

places.name: La Gaviota
places.note: Fried-fish house in the fishing quarter where locals go for volume and value.

food.name: Anchoas de Santona
food.desc: Salt-cured Cantabrian anchovy fillets hand-filleted in nearby Santona, laid on bread with butter or good olive oil. Nothing else needed.

places.name: Canadio
places.note: Emblematic Santander kitchen; artisan Santona anchovies are the signature bite.

places.name: Casa Lita
places.note: Pintxo bar on the waterfront with a counter of anchovy and seafood toasts.

places.name: Bodega del Riojano
places.note: Historic barrel-painted bodega serving classic Cantabrian conservas.

food.name: Cocido montanes
food.desc: The mountain stew: white beans slow-cooked with collard greens, chorizo, morcilla and pork belly. Winter food, served in two courses.

places.name: Bodega Fuente De
places.note: Cited in 2025 local guides for a full cocido montanes at a bargain price.

places.name: Bodega La Conveniente
places.note: Traditional bodega cooking; cocido and lebaniego turn up on the daily menu.

places.name: Bodega del Riojano
places.note: One of Santander's most characterful rooms for old-school Cantabrian plates.

food.name: Marmita de bonito
food.desc: Fisherman's stew of potato, pepper and onion with chunks of summer bonito, cooked on board and now a staple of the port kitchens.

places.name: La Gaviota
places.note: Port-side dining room built around whatever the boats landed that morning.

places.name: Marucho
places.note: Seasonal bonito dishes appear all summer beside the squid and clams.

places.name: Bodega del Riojano
places.note: Dependable version of the classic potato-and-tuna stew in the old centre.

food.name: Sobaos pasiegos
food.desc: Buttery sponge cakes from the Pas valleys, baked in paper cases and eaten at breakfast, dunked into coffee or milk.

places.name: Mercado de la Esperanza
places.note: Iron-framed 1904 market where stalls sell valley sobaos and quesada.

places.name: Mercado del Este
places.note: Restored market hall with delis stocking Pas dairy and regional bakes.

places.name: Regma
places.note: Long-running Cantabrian dairy shop, a local habit for sweets and ice cream.

food.name: Quesada pasiega
food.desc: Dense curd-and-butter tart scented with lemon and cinnamon, the region's default dessert and a common souvenir from the valleys.

places.name: Mercado de la Esperanza
places.note: Buy it by the slab from dairy stalls at the city's main food market.

places.name: Bodega La Conveniente
places.note: Turns up as the house dessert after the bodega's big raciones.

places.name: Bodega del Riojano
places.note: Traditional Cantabrian desserts close out a meal in the painted-barrel room.

food.name: Orujo de Liebana
food.desc: Fierce grape-pomace spirit from the Liebana valley, drunk neat or as sweet crema de orujo after a heavy Cantabrian meal.

places.name: Bodega del Riojano
places.note: Old bodega with the regional spirits you would expect after dinner.

places.name: Bodega La Conveniente
places.note: Orujo and herb liqueurs poured late in a rambling barrel-lined space.

places.name: Canadio
places.note: Serious bar list including local digestifs in the city's nightlife square.

food.name: Sidra cantabra
food.desc: Dry northern cider poured from a height to break the bubbles; Cantabria bottles its own alongside the better-known Asturian labels.

places.name: Bodega La Conveniente
places.note: Cider and vermouth by the glass in a big, noisy, thoroughly local room.

places.name: Casa Lita
places.note: Waterfront pintxo bar that pairs cider and txakoli with anchovy toasts.

places.name: Mercado del Este
places.note: Market-hall bars are an easy stop for a glass with a plate of rabas.

landmarks: Palacio de la Magdalena
An Edwardian-style royal summer palace commanding its own peninsula of headland paths, beaches and a small seal-and-penguin marine park.
Centro Botín
Renzo Piano's pearly twin-lobed arts centre hovers over the bay on pillars, pairing world-class exhibitions with rooftop waterfront views.
Playa de El Sardinero
A grand belle-epoque beach promenade of gardens and the historic Gran Casino, where Cantabrian surf meets aristocratic seaside elegance.
Catedral de Nuestra Señora de la Asunción
Two stacked Gothic churches form Santander's fortress-like cathedral, its 12th-century lower crypt sheltering relics of the city's martyr saints.
Paseo y Jardines de Pereda
Santander's classic waterfront gardens and promenade, lined with banks' grand facades and the beloved monument to novelist José María de Pereda.
Faro de Cabo Mayor
A clifftop lighthouse of 1839 guarding the bay's entrance, with dramatic coastal walks and an art centre inside the keeper's quarters.
Museo Marítimo del Cantábrico
Whale skeletons, aquarium tanks and centuries of seafaring heritage tell the story of Cantabria's intimate bond with the Bay of Biscay.
Mercado de la Esperanza
A splendid iron-and-glass 1904 market behind the town hall, piled each morning with anchovies, sardines and Cantabrian cheeses.
Parque de la Naturaleza de Cabárceno
A vast former iron mine reimagined as a semi-wild reserve where elephants, bears and giraffes roam surreal karst landscapes.
El Capricho de Gaudí (Comillas)
Gaudí's playful sunflower-tiled villa of 1885 crowns the nearby seaside town of Comillas, an easy and rewarding coastal day trip.

train.note: No international trains. Renfe long-distance services reach Madrid in about 4h30, and the narrow-gauge Renfe Feve line runs the slow, scenic Cantabrian coastal route west to Oviedo and east toward Bilbao. Both use the combined station beside the ferry terminal in the middle of town. Booking opens around 60 days ahead.

bus.note: The bus station is next to the railway station and ferry terminal, which makes connections easy. ALSA runs frequently to Bilbao (about 1h20), Oviedo and Madrid, and buses are usually faster than the coastal Feve trains. Carry your passport for international services.

intl.to: Plymouth (UK) - ~20 hr across the Bay of Biscay

ferry.note: Santander's ferry terminal is right in the city centre beside the railway and bus stations, which is unusual and very convenient. Brittany Ferries sails to Plymouth and Portsmouth several times a week, mostly overnight, with cabins compulsory on the longer crossings. It is the main way British drivers reach northern Spain without the long drive through France, so summer sailings book up months in advance.

half.name: Santillana del Mar
half.blurb: A medieval village of cobbled streets and stone manor houses, often called one of Spain's best-preserved historic towns.

half.name: Cuevas de Altamira
half.blurb: A museum and replica cave near Santillana del Mar recreating the prehistoric bison paintings from the original Paleolithic cave nearby.

half.name: Castro Urdiales
half.blurb: A fishing town with a Gothic church perched on a cliff, a Roman-era lighthouse, and a medieval bridge over the harbor.

full.name: Picos de Europa National Park
full.blurb: A limestone mountain range with jagged peaks, gorges, and the Fuente Dé cable car climbing to alpine viewpoints.
